title: Beha'alotcha: until it rises alone (Numbers 8:2)
hook: Rashi: Aaron holds the light to the wick until the flame rises by itself

segments.voice: Yesterday twelve leaders brought twelve identical gifts, and your line was each gift counted in full. Did someone get thanked as if they were the only one? Day four hundred forty-one.

A birthday cake, a draft from the window, one match. You touch the match to the wick. The wick blackens, smokes, takes a tiny blue bead of flame. Pull the match away too soon and it dies. So you wait, holding steady, until the flame stands up on its own and doesn't need you anymore. Then you let go. That small, patient moment is how the commentator Rashi explains the word this week's portion is named for. And he turns it into a picture of what a teacher does.
screen: `A MATCH TO A WICK.` → `TOO SOON, IT DIES.` → `WAIT TILL IT STANDS ALONE.`

segments.voice: God tells Moses to speak to Aaron: "When thou lightest the lamps," the seven lamps of the menorah shall give light toward its front. In Hebrew, when thou lightest is beha'alotcha, and it doesn't literally say light. It says when you raise up, when you make it go up. Rashi asks why. His answer, from the ancient rabbis: because the flame goes upward. Aaron must hold the light to each wick until the flame rises by itself. Rashi has a second comment that connects to yesterday. Why does this section come right after the leaders' twelve gifts? Because, the midrash says, Aaron felt left out. Every tribe had a leader at the dedication, and his tribe, Levi, brought nothing. So God told him: yours is greater than theirs. They brought gifts once. You will light and tend the lamps. A gift is given and done. A flame has to be kept. And then the verse says, simply: and Aaron did so. Rashi reads that as praise. He didn't change a thing; he did it exactly, day after day. The image is often borrowed for teaching. You don't light someone by grabbing their wick and holding it forever. You don't light them by touching it once and walking away. You stay close, steady, until the light is theirs. Then you step back, and the flame keeps going up.
screen: `BEHA'ALOTCHA: WHEN YOU RAISE UP.` · `HOLD IT TILL IT RISES ALONE.` · `A GIFT IS ONCE. A FLAME IS KEPT.` · `AND AARON DID SO.` · then, large: `UNTIL IT RISES ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help someone catch their own flame. Breathe, and think of someone just starting something: a kid learning to cook, a new coworker, a friend trying to quit something, a student stuck on a problem. Ask honestly: am I pulling the match away too soon, or holding it there so long that it never becomes theirs? Picture one small way to stay close a little longer, and one way to let go a little sooner. The bell holds the time.

Beha'alotcha. When you raise up: the lamp held until it burns alone. This week: cover what's holy, counting is lifting, repay and add a fifth, a vow for a season, the priests' blessing, each gift counted in full, and now this.
Your line: until it rises alone. Today, stay with someone through one hard first try, then step back and let it be theirs. Day four hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Beha'alotcha is read in early summer; Rashi's comments on its first verse, that the flame must be held until it rises by itself, and that Aaron's tending of the lamps outshone the leaders' gifts, are often taught as a picture of teaching and patience.

original.note: Hebrew: when you raise up. the word for lighting the menorah's lamps.

trapdoor: what you thought: Aaron simply lit the lamps.
what it means: he held the light to each wick until the flame rose by itself.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on Numbers 8:2, from the Sifrei and Talmud Shabbat 21a, reads raise up as kindling until the flame climbs on its own.
